title: OpenAI Makes Stunning Financial Move Ahead of Potential IPO - TradingView
content: Microsoft MSFT backed OpenAI has reportedly lowered its valuation target to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion as some investors push back against the price of its latest funding round. The AI company is now seeking up to $30 billion in fresh capital at the lower pre-money valuation, according to a report cited by TipRanks. Investors from the United Arab Emirates are expected to lead the round, while Coatue is also expected to participate. The change represents a $150 billion reduction from OpenAI's previously reported target, though the new figure remains well above the company's roughly $852 billion valuation in March 2026. The reason appears to be a more cautious funding environment. TipRanks said investor demand has been weaker than in previous rounds as concerns grow around the enormous cost of building AI infrastructure and whether those investments will ultimately generate sufficient returns. Some investors may also be dealing with funding fatigue after pouring large sums into AI companies over the past several years. That concern is showing up elsewhere in the market. Meta Platforms recently came under pressure despite beating revenue estimates after increasing the lower end of its 2026 capital-spending outlook to $135 billion from $130 billion, while keeping the upper end at $145 billion. OpenAI itself has told investors it expects to spend roughly $600 billion on computing by 2030, highlighting just how capital-intensive its growth plans have become. The company is also reportedly exploring additional computing capacity through a commercial arrangement with the UAE. I think the valuation cut matters less because OpenAI is suddenly worth dramatically less and more because it shows AI investors are becoming more price-sensitive. But the fact that OpenAI reportedly had to move down from $1.4 trillion suggests investors are no longer willing to fund AI growth at almost any price. That is particularly important when the company could spend around $600 billion on compute through 2030. For investors, the key things to watch are how much OpenAI ultimately raises, the final valuation, the terms of the round, compute spending and whether the company can show operating leverage before a potential 2027 IPO. But the cost of capital is starting to matter a lot more. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. Select reference data provided by FactSet. title: Could You Have Seen The Run In Microsoft Stock Coming? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Microsoft (MSFT) stock returned 36.8% from July 24 to October 22, 2026, against 3.7% for the S&P 500. This rally followed a period where the shares had lost 17.7% over the six months before July 24. By the end of this run, investors were paying a much higher price for the same twelve months of Microsoft’s earnings. What had Microsoft told investors before July 24? Well over a year before the run, management told investors that customers were buying more. On its January 29, 2025 call, management said large companies were beginning to move from small trials to “enterprise-wide deployments”, and that commercial bookings, the contracts customers sign for future sales, had increased 67%, a jump the finance chief said was driven by Azure commitments from OpenAI. Six months later, on the July 30, 2025 call, management said Azure, its cloud platform, had passed $75 billion in annual revenue, up 34%. This expansion was more than twice the 14.9% growth Microsoft reported as a whole for fiscal 2025. Company filings reinforced these statements. Microsoft’s revenue growth from a year earlier rose from 13.3% in the quarter ended March 2025 to 18.1% in the quarter ended June 2025. Growth was still 18.3% in the quarter ended March 2026, which Microsoft filed on April 29, 2026, before the run. The evidence was public and held steady, but the shares still lost 17.7% in the six months before July 24. How Much More Investors Now Pay For Microsoft’s Earnings At the October 22 close, investors paid 28.9 times Microsoft’s earnings for the twelve months to June 2026, against 20.7 times at the end of June. The end-of-June multiple was the lowest at any quarter end since fiscal 2017. The business maintained the pace shown in its earlier filings. In the quarter ended June 2026, Microsoft’s revenue was $90.0 billion, up 17.7% from a year earlier. The shares rose 15.5% on July 30, 2026, marking the biggest one-day move of the run. Microsoft’s performance diverged notably from its mega-cap peers over this three-month span. Alphabet, Amazon and Apple stock each returned 7.9% or less over the same three months. On sales, yes. Microsoft’s revenue grew between 16.7% and 18.4% from a year earlier in each of the four quarters to June 2026, much the same pace the filings showed before the run. Profit on each dollar of those sales has slipped, however. Microsoft’s operating margin fell in each of the last three quarters, dropping from 48.9% in the quarter ended September 2025 to 45.1% in the quarter ended June 2026. This figure remained above the 44.9% of a year earlier. Over the full twelve months, the margin was still 46.8%, against 18.5% for the S&P 500 taken as one company. Microsoft is expected to report next on October 28, 2026, and its revenue growth from a year earlier is the number to watch. Your Advisor Retired? We came across a bullish thesis on Alphabet Inc. on Astute Optics - US's Substack. In this article, we will summarize the bulls' thesis on GOOGL. Alphabet Inc.'s share was trading at $334.76 as of October 21st 2026. GOOGL's trailing and forward P/E were 17.62 and 22.83 respectively according to Yahoo Finance. This isn't the first time we see a technology company pitched as a great investment. GOOGL shares gained 35.20% over the last 12 months. Comparable stocks like Amazon gained 20.50% during the same period. Strong gains can attract investors, but GOOGL's recent pullback raises a different question: has the weakness created a buying opportunity, or is there more reason for caution? In July, we published an article about the 10 Best Quantum Computing Stocks to Buy and Hold Forever and GOOGL ranked #3 in that article. While GOOGL has edged slightly lower since then, the #1 stock in that list returned 41.18% over the same period. So, hedge funds were right about their #1 pick while GOOGL's performance has been more subdued. This article explains why hedge funds were bullish on GOOGL. Before getting into our analysis, let's take a look at the business and why some investors like the stock so much. Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) provides internet services and technology platforms through Google Services, Google Cloud, and Other Bets. Its core business still centers on Google Search, YouTube, Android, Chrome, Maps, and advertising, but the real question for investors is whether artificial intelligence and cloud computing can become its next big growth drivers. Over the past year, revenue reached $445.9 billion, up 20.1%, and profitability improved as well, with margins climbing to healthy levels. The stock trades below the industry average on a headline basis, which on the surface makes it look cheaper than peers — though once one-time gains are stripped out, the valuation looks closer to the sector average. In short, the market isn't just paying for what Alphabet Inc. earns today; it's betting on years of AI and cloud-driven growth ahead. Read More: 15 AI Stocks That Are Quietly Making Investors Rich Read More: Undervalued AI Stock Poised For Massive Gains: 10000% Upside Potential The bullish case is that Alphabet Inc. can use its massive existing user base to turn AI into real revenue across multiple businesses. Google Search keeps driving advertising income, while Google Cloud is emerging as a fast-growing enterprise business as companies adopt AI tools and Gemini-based products. Recent results back this up: quarterly revenue grew 24% year over year to $119.8 billion, and Google Cloud revenue jumped 82% to $24.8 billion as businesses ramped up spending on AI infrastructure. If that trend continues, bulls believe Alphabet Inc. can grow both from higher cloud demand and new ways to monetize AI across its platforms. The company is backing this optimism with money: it raised its capital spending plans to a range of $195 billion to $205 billion to build out data centers and AI capacity. It can afford to, given a net cash position of $144.3 billion and $164.7 billion in operating cash flow last fiscal year. That financial cushion means Alphabet Inc. can keep funding its AI buildout without straining its balance sheet, which supports the bull case that this could be a multi-year growth story rather than a single strong quarter. You can check out whether Amazon or Alphabet makes the stronger AI cloud investment case after the spending bill here. Wall Street largely shares that optimism. The average analyst price target of $422 implies roughly 26% upside from current levels, with estimates ranging widely depending on how much credit analysts give to AI and cloud growth. For that upside to materialize, though, Alphabet Inc. will need to keep converting its AI investments into actual earnings growth — if that monetization slows, these expectations could prove too optimistic. The biggest risk is that all this spending doesn't pay off fast enough. If AI is truly opening a new growth cycle, investors will expect the money being poured into infrastructure to eventually show up as stronger profits. Rising capital spending adds execution risk, and regulatory scrutiny over search and advertising practices could threaten some of Alphabet Inc.'s most profitable businesses. On top of that, newer AI-powered search tools are creating fresh uncertainty about the long-term strength of its core advertising model. Another risk for the stock is businesses cutting advertising budgets when economic conditions weaken. Google can retain its users and search traffic while advertisers spend less to reach them. Alphabet generated more than 70% of its revenue from online advertising in 2025, leaving it heavily exposed to those spending decisions. Weaker consumer demand could prompt advertisers to reduce campaigns or lower their bids. That would pressure advertising revenue even without Google losing market share to AI competitors. Cloud growth may not fully offset a slowdown across its much larger advertising business. In our opinion, this dependence could pressure Alphabet's price multiples if advertising weakens before newer businesses contribute enough profit. Hedge fund positioning shows a mixed signal. As per our database, 275 hedge funds held Alphabet Inc. at the end of the second quarter, up from 265 the quarter before — a modest increase suggesting institutional investors remain generally confident in its AI and cloud story despite valuation and regulatory concerns. By comparison, Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) was held by 273 hedge funds, down from 282, Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN) was held by 369 hedge funds, up from 353, and Meta Platforms Inc. was held by 254 hedge funds, down from 262. Amazon.com Inc. clearly saw the strongest jump in institutional interest, while Alphabet Inc. gained ground compared with Microsoft Corporation and Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META), pointing to continued confidence in large-cap tech names tied to AI. Short interest data also paints a fairly calm picture. About 1.37% of Alphabet Inc.'s float is sold short, versus 0.82% for Microsoft Corporation, 0.88% for Amazon.com, Inc., and 1.52% for Meta Platforms, Inc. That's higher than Microsoft Corporation and Amazon.com, Inc. but slightly below Meta Platforms, Inc., suggesting some investors are watching Alphabet Inc.'s spending, valuation, and regulatory risks more closely than those of Microsoft Corporation and Amazon.com, Inc. Even so, short interest remains low across all four companies, suggesting limited outright bearish conviction across the group. GOOGL's forward P/E is 22.83x. Microsoft Corporation, Amazon.com, Inc., and Meta Platforms, Inc. trade at forward P/Es of 25.13x, 23.64x, and 22.08x, respectively. GOOGL's own forward P/E was 28.01x on December 31, 2025, meaning its current valuation is approximately 18% lower. We believe the current valuation reflects significant investor concerns about rising AI spending, competition in search, and regulatory pressure. However, its modest discounts to Microsoft and Amazon and slight premium to Meta suggest the stock is reasonably priced rather than deeply undervalued. Alphabet Inc.'s trailing revenue increased 20.1% to $445.9 billion, while second-quarter revenue grew approximately 24%, although large investment gains inflated reported profits and should not be treated as recurring earnings growth. We believe Alphabet can justify 22.83 times forward earnings if its advertising and cloud businesses sustain double-digit earnings growth after rising infrastructure costs, allowing shareholder returns without requiring a higher P/E. If Alphabet turns AI demand into lasting profits and maintains sufficient cash flow after capital spending, the current valuation could offer an attractive entry point despite its execution and regulatory risks. GOOGL's stock price has appreciated by approximately 111.2% since our coverage. We believe GOOGL could be a good long-term investment, as its reasonable valuation offers an attractive entry point if advertising and cloud growth sustain double-digit earnings growth after rising AI costs. Not many people remember this, but when Satya Nadella took the reins as CEO of Microsoft in February 2014, the company was struggling to find its place amidst a tech landscape dominated by Apple's smartphones, Google's Android operating system, and Amazon's cloud computing services. Under the leadership of Steve Ballmer, Microsoft had undertaken a contentious $7.2 billion acquisition of Nokia's mobile phone business in 2013. That deal ultimately failed, resulting in billions in write-downs and thousands of layoffs. But Nadella did not turn the company around overnight. Over the next few years, he shifted Microsoft's business model even further into cloud computing by expanding Azure and its subscription-based services. He also made strategic acquisitions, including LinkedIn, GitHub, and Minecraft, while investing billions into artificial intelligence before it became a household name. In fact, you could say that Nadella was instrumental in Microsoft's partnership with OpenAI, as he even personally stepped in to serve as mediator when OpenAI's board briefly fired its CEO and co-founder, Sam Altman, in the fall of 2023. Although Microsoft and OpenAI renegotiated their once-exclusive partnership, Microsoft hasn't lost momentum. Their newest agreement, announced in April 2026, gave each greater independence and allowed Microsoft to continue to expand its own AI capabilities through Azure's cloud services. MSFT crossed the trillion-dollar valuation threshold on April 25, 2019, and it hasn't looked back since. In its most recent earnings, the company reported that Azure revenue grew by 43% year-over-year. These results show that Microsoft isn't just one of the founders of the digital era — it's very much a power player, and as the driver behind its innovation, Nadella himself has been rewarded handsomely through salary increases, bonuses, and enormous stock awards. As of Microsoft's latest Proxy statement for fiscal 2025, filed in September 2025, Satya Nadella owned 900,572 shares of Microsoft, equating to about 0.01% of the company's total outstanding shares. Given MSFT's October 19 closing share price of $533.52, those shares would be worth a whopping $480.4 million. But Nadella isn't Microsoft's biggest individual shareholder — not by a long shot. That distinction actually belongs to Steve Ballmer, who is estimated to still own approximately 319 million shares, or roughly 4% of Microsoft. Despite Ballmer stepping down amid Microsoft's struggles, he still owns more than 350 times as much as Nadella's stake. And in case you're wondering, even Microsoft's founder Bill Gates still owns about 103 million shares, valued at approximately $43 billion. That's substantially more than Nadella — even though Gates has spent decades giving away his fortune. Related: How much MSFT stock does Microsoft founder Bill Gates actually own? To say that Microsoft's board of directors has been happy with Nadella's efforts is an understatement. In the company's latest Proxy statement, published in October 2025, the board stated that "Our exceptional fiscal year 2025 results demonstrate that Satya Nadella and his leadership team have positioned Microsoft as a clear artificial intelligence leader for this generational technology shift, enabling Microsoft to drive long-term growth through innovation, security, and quality." Crediting Nadella for the company's 15% annual revenue growth and 17% increase in operating income, the esteemed CEO received a 117.00% payout in annual cash incentives and a 103.69% payout in performance stock awards. The $96.5 million compensation Nadella received in fiscal 2025 was an increase of about 22% from fiscal 2024, when he made $79.1 million. Agnes Heftberger, chair of the management board of Microsoft Germany, said in the release that Volkswagen is "putting AI directly into the flow of work." Fortune counted 16 companies that have formally objected, and reported that Microsoft was among those that declined to comment or did not respond. title: What Did It Take To Hold Microsoft Stock? - Trefis
content: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com. Over the last ten years, Microsoft (MSFT) stock turned $10,000 into $92,451 before dividends. That same $10,000 invested in the S&P 500 became $35,968. Looking back makes the strategy seem as simple as buying and waiting, but holding the shares required far more discipline. How many times do you think Microsoft stock fell 20% or more along the way? Microsoft stock fell 20% or more from a closing high four times. Two of those declines exceeded 30%. All four are listed below. Falls of 20% or more from a closing high, Oct 2016 to Oct 2026. Split-adjusted closing prices, dividends excluded. The deepest drop occurred between November 2021 and November 2022, when the stock fell 37.6% while the S&P 500 lost 20.8%. Investors spent about 19 months below the previous peak until the shares closed above that old high in June 2023. The real question was never just whether to buy Microsoft. It was whether you could sit through falls like these. What Did Holding Microsoft Through A Fall Feel Like? The most recent decline began at a closing high on October 28, 2025, and the stock took nearly eight months to reach its low on June 25, 2026, dropping 34.9%. The S&P 500 rose 6.8% over those same months, so shareholders lost ground while the broader market gained. From that low, the stock took another 3.6 months to close above its old high. All four of Microsoft’s declines eventually ended. Nobody holding shares in the middle of a drop knew that at the time, however, and an investor in the spring of 2026 had no way to know this one would. Microsoft generates revenue from cloud services such as Azure and software such as Microsoft 365. Its two largest segments are Intelligent Cloud, followed by Productivity and Business Processes. During the deepest fall, revenue over twelve months rose 15.2%, and the operating margin stayed close to 42% from the high to the low. In the latest fall, which was shorter, twelve-month revenue rose 8.3% from the high to the low, and the operating margin edged up from 46.3% to 46.8%. Sales grew and operating margins held steady during both falls while the stock declined. A drop like that, while the business keeps growing, is the risk of holding the shares. Microsoft stock is up 148.2% since its November 2022 low, and anyone who sold there missed all of it. Today, the stock sits 2.1% below the high it set on October 13, 2026. Enduring those four falls was the cost of the ten-year gain, and the investors who captured those returns were the ones who sat through every drop. Microsoft’s revenue kept growing during both the deepest decline and the latest one. The next time Microsoft stock falls hard, check whether its revenue is falling with it. Not necessarily on Microsoft alone, if your goal is long-term wealth. Wealth is built by owning the companies that keep outperforming, the leaders of their industries, wherever they are.
